approach.label: How I work
approach.body: I don't hand off sketches and hope. I run the interviews, synthesise the signals, draft the IA, prototype the interactions, then sit beside real users and watch it break. The work only counts when it ships.

1.b: Field notes, transcripts, task evidence, and the quiet signals people almost miss.

2.b: Affinity maps, JTBD, tree tests — structured reasoning.

3.b: Figma, Framer, HTML/CSS/React — I build at the fidelity needed.

4.b: Usability test, iterate, hand off with rationale intact.

hero.title: UQ Connect
hero.sub: Rebuilding the information architecture of a student portal serving 50,000 students.

ch.label: The problem
ch.title: Twelve top-level categories, most of them opaque.
ch.p: New students arrived at a portal written in staff-facing language — "HiQ", "SI-net", "mySI-net" — and had to guess. The search bar didn't forgive typos or synonyms. The mobile experience collapsed to a hamburger that hid 80+ links.

re.label: Research
re.title: Three methods, one month.

m1.b: Students grouped and named the portal's most common tasks in their own words.

m2.b: Task-based sessions on the live portal, watching where people gave up or left for Google.

m3.b: The existing structure against two alternative trees.

re.quote: I just Google 'UQ how to drop a subject'. I never start on the portal.

sy.label: Synthesis
sy.title: The portal was organised by who owns the information, not who needs it.
sy.p: Affinity mapping revealed that student mental models clustered around five life-stages: arriving, studying, belonging, supporting myself, moving on. We collapsed twelve staff-oriented buckets into six task-oriented ones, with "I'm new" promoted to the front door.

id.label: IA decisions
id.p: Three alternative trees were tested; the winning one preserved a fallback alphabetical index for power users while leading with the task-first structure. Every category name went through a plain-language review with two non-UQ reviewers.

pr.label: Prototype
pr.p: A Figma prototype covered the top 15 tasks end-to-end at mid-fidelity. The navigation shell and the "I'm new" landing were built to high fidelity to validate reading flow on mobile.

te.label: Usability test
te.p: Moderated remote sessions surfaced a naming collision between "Money" and "My account" that had only shown up at high fidelity — renamed on the spot, and the re-run confirmed people stopped hesitating there.

ou.label: What it produced
ou.p: The deliverable was a tested information architecture: a task-first tree, plain-language category names, and a mid-fidelity prototype covering the top tasks end to end. Evidence status — this is university project work, not a shipped portal. I can walk through the card-sort groupings, the tree-test tasks, and why each category name changed; I have not measured impact on the live product.

rf.label: Reflection
rf.p: The research phase was longer than planned — I would budget for that again. The most valuable decision was insisting on a plain-language review from non-UQ readers; it caught four category names that sounded fine to anyone steeped in the institution.

hero.title: Spectra Lens
hero.sub: Letting colourblind users read the world on their own time.

ch.label: The problem
ch.title: Eight percent of men see the world in fewer colours — and almost every app assumes they don't.
ch.p: Traffic signals, food freshness, data dashboards, medication — everyday tasks silently assume full colour perception. For the 8% of men and 0.5% of women with colour vision deficiency, each one becomes a small negotiation: memorise a workaround, ask a stranger, or guess. Existing tools felt clinical and stigmatising — built for a clinic, not a Tuesday morning.

re.label: Research
re.title: One persistent answer, from three directions.

m1.b: Semi-structured sessions across CVD subtypes (deuter-, protan-, tritan-anomaly).

m2.b: Existing colour-ID tools judged against accessibility and social-friction criteria.

m3.b: Sessions mapping daily colour moments, then rapid sketch-ideation.

re.quote: The moment I pull out the app, the conversation stops. I'd rather guess than explain.

sy.label: Synthesis
sy.title: Users don't need the colour named — they need the decision made.
sy.p: Three themes dominated the interviews: speed (a colour decision has a short window before it feels awkward to bystanders), context (users want to know if the food is bad, not that it's 'muddy green'), and privacy (most don't want to identify as colourblind in public). Every app I reviewed optimised for naming colours. None optimised for acting on them.

id.label: Design decisions
id.p: We chose an AR overlay over a full-screen filter because the overlay preserves context — users still see the world, just with a low-opacity annotation layer. Audio feedback became opt-in rather than default after co-design sessions flagged public audibility of the app as a concern. The whole interaction was compressed to a single-tap camera mode: no menu, no account, no colour dictionary to memorise.

pr.label: Prototype
pr.p: A Figma high-fidelity prototype simulated realistic AR camera behaviour, with three feedback modes (overlay, audio, haptic) and a one-screen settings surface. We deliberately kept a 'quick mode' for the most common scenarios (traffic, clothing, food) to test whether discoverability or depth mattered more.

te.label: Usability test
te.p: Moderated sessions in real environments — a cafeteria, a pedestrian crossing, participants' own wardrobes. The overlay's initial opacity obscured texture detail in food, so I lowered it and added haptic confirmation. In noisy places, voice feedback was slower than simply reading the overlay, and participants preferred a silent default with audio as a toggle.

ou.label: What it produced
ou.p: The deliverable was a high-fidelity AR prototype and the interaction model behind it: annotate rather than filter, answer the decision rather than name the hue, and never make the user announce their colour vision in public. Evidence status — university project work with a small, self-recruited sample. The direction is supported by what those participants did in context; it has not been validated at scale or with clinical measures.

rf.label: Reflection
rf.p: AR accessibility is still under-served because 'accessibility' is too often read as 'screen reader'. The biggest lesson was cognitive load — every piece of information the overlay added was a piece the user had to ignore later. Next time I'd prototype the zero-state (what the camera looks like when it says nothing) before designing the affordances.

hero.title: AI Interview Assistant
hero.sub: Rehearsing the hardest conversation of your career — without an audience.

ai.teamVal: Solo, with input from two career counsellors

ch.label: The problem
ch.title: Candidates don't fail on content. They fail on nerves — and coaching costs money.
ch.p: Interview prep has a clear market divide: senior candidates pay for coaches, everyone else reads question lists. Survey respondents told me that nervousness, not content, was the thing standing between them and a job. Existing platforms optimised for either peer practice (unreliable quality) or video courses (no feedback loop). Nobody was tackling the emotional shape of the problem.

re.label: Research
re.title: A survey, interviews, and a teardown of the incumbents.

m1.b: Cross-seniority questions on preparation habits and pain points.

m2.b: In-depth sessions with recent interviewees — both offered and still searching.

m3.b: Pramp, Yoodli, Big Interview, Google Interview Warmup and others, read for what they optimise.

re.quote: I know what to say. I just can't say it with someone watching.

sy.label: Synthesis
sy.title: Content is table stakes. The product has to manage anxiety.
sy.p: The critical insight was that anxiety, not knowledge, gated performance. Users wanted realistic practice — not robotic — but didn't want to be judged while being wrong. That meant two things: the AI persona had to be warmer than a recruiter, and feedback had to arrive after the session, never mid-sentence. Every competitor we reviewed violated one of these.

id.label: Design decisions
id.p: Three non-negotiables: a named AI persona ("Alex") with natural pacing and pause, post-session feedback by default, and three session-length presets (5 / 10 / 20 min) rather than open-ended. We explicitly rejected body-language analysis after research showed it deepened the self-consciousness that was already the problem.

pr.label: Prototype
pr.p: An interactive Figma prototype simulated the full loop: voice input via speech-to-text, three interview types (behavioural, technical, case), and a detailed post-session report with a calibrated tone — constructive framing, specific rather than generic praise. A 'confidence boost' mode offered easier questions for users who wanted a ramp before a real session.

te.label: Usability test
te.p: Moderated sessions over two weeks, plus a side-by-side comparison of feedback timing — inline versus post-session. Post-session was preferred clearly and consistently; inline feedback was experienced as interruption even when the content was useful. Participants also asked the AI to pause longer between questions, so I added a natural beat.

ou.label: What it produced
ou.p: The deliverable was an interaction model for AI coaching: when the system speaks, how it frames a weakness, and where it deliberately stays quiet. The timing finding was the most useful result, because it is a principle rather than a feature. Evidence status — university project work; the preference for post-session feedback comes from a small moderated sample, and I have not run it as a controlled experiment or measured real interview outcomes.

rf.label: Reflection
rf.p: Designing with AI isn't designing a chatbot; it's designing a relationship. The persona's warmth, pacing, and word choice did more work than any single feature. The next direction I'd push is emotional calibration — letting users set how gentle or rigorous the session feels, not as a difficulty slider but as a tone.

hero.title: Connect Circles
hero.sub: Friendship by quality, not quantity — a slow-match app for international students.

circles.teamVal: Solo, with co-design alongside international students

ch.label: The problem
ch.title: Loneliness in the first semester is common — and the apps make it worse.
ch.p: Moving countries for study collapses an entire social scaffolding. Language barriers, unfamiliar norms, and academic pressure combine so that meeting new people feels simultaneously urgent and exhausting. The apps students use — Meetup, Bumble BFF, Hey! VINA — optimise for matching volume, exactly the metric that scales the emotional cost. The students I spoke to said they'd rather have one deep friendship than ten casual matches, and no existing product was designed around that preference.

re.label: Research
re.title: Three cultural regions, three methods, one stubborn pattern.

m1.b: Semi-structured sessions across East Asian, South Asian, and European student cohorts.

m2.b: Two weeks logging social interactions and how participants felt before and after each one.

m3.b: Workshops on ideal features, dealbreakers, and cultural considerations.

re.quote: I don't want more friends. I want one person I can stop pretending around.

sy.label: Synthesis
sy.title: The market is built on volume. Users are asking for depth.
sy.p: Four themes held across cultures: depth beats breadth; shared vulnerability is the formation mechanism; first meetings need a shared activity, not a coffee date; and socialising norms vary enough that any one default will alienate someone. The design implication is almost the opposite of a dating app — slow down, give fewer matches, make them earn the next step.

id.label: Design decisions
id.p: Four directions were shortlisted from co-design: small-group 'circles' of three to five people (not pairs), structured vulnerability prompts to accelerate closeness, cultural-bridge hints on communication style, and slow matching with gradual information reveal. Real-time chat was deliberately de-scoped from v1 — the hypothesis is that less messaging and more shared context produces stronger ties.

pr.label: Prototype
pr.p: The next prototype scope is defined around onboarding (preference and comfort capture), circle match demonstration, activity suggestions with RSVP, in-app conversation prompts, and post-activity reflection. It is privacy-preserving by default — no public profile, no swipe surface.

te.label: Testing plan
te.p: The next validation step is preference testing and moderated usability sessions with target cohorts. The primary measure is not only usability, but perceived safety, cultural fit, and willingness to actually use the product across an eight-week window.

ou.label: Current state
ou.p: Research and synthesis are complete; the case defines the product direction, prototype scope, and validation plan. Evidence status — this is an in-progress research-through-design project. Nothing has been built or tested with users yet, so everything here is a stated hypothesis rather than a result, and the validation plan above is the honest next step.

rf.label: Reflection
rf.p: Designing for social wellbeing is the first time I've had to actively refuse growth metrics. Every conventional indicator — matches, messages, session time — works against the goal. The hardest design question right now is what the north-star metric should be when the desired outcome is 'one good friendship over a semester', and how to instrument for that without turning a relationship into a KPI.

hero.title: MazeRunners
hero.sub: A physical maze wired so that a ball, a score, a buzz on your finger, and a browser console all describe the same moment.

maze.teamVal: Team project; I owned firmware, sensing, feedback, and the web console
maze.toolsVal: Arduino Mega · Arduino C/C++ · FC-51 IR · TM1637 · Web Serial · JS Canvas

ch.label: The problem
ch.title: A maze is furniture until it answers you.
ch.p: The brief was a physical maze game for a public exhibition. The failure mode showed up in the first build: a nice object that people pushed a ball around while nothing happened. Scoring lived in someone's head, traps were painted lines, and the only feedback was other players laughing. The design problem was not the maze — it was making the system notice events and answer them fast enough that a stranger learns the rules without being told.

re.label: Groundwork
re.title: Working out what the system must sense, and what it must never do.

m1.b: Ten FC-51 IR sensors assigned across trap, diagnostic, spare, and finish zones, each needing its own trigger behaviour.

m2.b: The original trap concept was a mild electric shock. Unsupervised exhibition play made per-person consent and calibration impossible.

m3.b: Score, timer, vibration, lights, audio, and a browser console — each a channel that could carry or muddy the same event.

re.quote: People don't read the score display. They feel the buzz and look up.

sy.label: System concept
sy.title: One event, many channels, one round state machine.
sy.p: Everything hangs off a single round state machine. A ball breaks an IR beam, round state advances, and that one event fans out: score and timer displays update, a vibration pulse fires in the player's finger sleeve, the LED strip and speaker respond, and the browser console logs it. Subsystems reacting independently is exactly what made the first build feel like unrelated gadgets screwed to plywood.

id.label: Technical decisions
id.p: Vibration replaced the electric shock: relay-driven motors in wearable finger sleeves keep the sensation on the body without a risk that needs supervision. Each IR sensor got debounce and a cooldown window, because raw reads double- and triple-fired on a single pass and broke agreement between score, timer, and haptics. Platform tilt moved to its own SafeTouchServoController with hold-to-move behaviour, so servo motion stopped competing with time-sensitive sensor polling and a servo fault could not take down the round.

pr.label: The web console
pr.p: A browser-based system console connects over Web Serial and mirrors the maze live: score and timer HUD, hardware bay, event log, and feedback simulation on a canvas. It also runs standalone in demo mode, because the hardware is not in the room during development — or in a portfolio, or an interview. Regression tests cover serial sync, feedback sync, servo response, and audio parity so the demo cannot quietly drift away from what the firmware does.

te.label: Testing and iteration
te.p: Bench testing tuned debounce and cooldown until one ball pass produced exactly one game event. Parity tests caught drift whenever the firmware or the console was edited alone. Group play at the exhibition then surfaced what the bench could not: players reacted to vibration and audio faster than to the score display, and the finger sleeves had to be fitted for people rather than self-fitted — the setup ritual turned out to be part of the interaction.

ou.label: What it produced
ou.p: A working, exhibited system: firmware modules for game state, IR sensing, player chain input, vibration and audio; a two-controller hardware split; and a browser console with parity tests. Evidence status — this is a university project built for one exhibition. Play was observed, not instrumented, so I can describe what players reacted to but cannot quantify which channel carried the most information.

rf.label: Reflection
rf.p: The strongest lesson was that on hardware, timing is design. Debounce sounds like an electronics detail until a double-fire makes the score disagree with the buzz on your finger, and the player stops trusting the system. The weakest part is that I proved the loop works without measuring which parts of it mattered — rebuilding it, I would log every sensor event and feedback fire from day one, then start switching channels off to find out which ones players were actually using.

about.p1: I'm finishing my Master of Interaction Design at the University of Queensland. Before that, I spent four years in a different discipline entirely, which is to say I got used to being the person in the room who has to translate between strangers.
about.p2: My work sits where research, architecture and craft overlap. I'm most useful on messy, high-stakes problems — the ones where nobody agrees what the product should be yet — because I enjoy the part everyone else finds tedious: reading interview transcripts at 1am until the pattern shows up.
about.p3: Outside the studio I cook with too much garlic, read non-fiction about cities, and occasionally attempt to learn Japanese. I reply to every email that isn't a recruiter mass-send.

1.b: If a study didn't change the design, the study wasn't necessary.

2.b: The best interaction is the one the user never notices solving their problem.

3.b: Empty states, errors, load states — that's where respect for the user lives.

4.b: A memo survives the meeting. A whiteboard doesn't.
